title: Stare Decisis and the Limits of Precedent
text:
The doctrine of stare decisis obliges courts to follow precedent in cases that raise materially identical facts. Its purpose is to promote predictability, since litigants can rely on settled rules when they plan their affairs. Yet the doctrine is not absolute, and appellate courts may overrule an earlier decision when its reasoning has proved unworkable.

Critics argue that rigid adherence to precedent can entrench errors that a later court would recognise as mistaken. Defenders reply that a court which revisits every question each time it arises would undermine the stability on which commercial life depends. The tension between these positions lies at the heart of much appellate reasoning.

questions.text: What does the doctrine of stare decisis require courts to do?
options: to follow precedent in cases with materially identical facts
to decide every case by a jury vote
to avoid written reasoning in their decisions

questions.text: What do defenders of strict adherence to precedent say revisiting every question would undermine?
options: the number of judges in the court
the stability on which commercial life depends

questions.text: Why might an appellate court overrule an earlier decision?
options: because its reasoning has proved unworkable
because the litigants are unhappy with the outcome
because the earlier judge was younger
because the case was settled quickly

questions.text: What does the passage suggest about the tension between the two positions?
options: it is central to much appellate reasoning
it has been fully resolved by statute
it is irrelevant to commercial law

vocabulary.translation: a previous decision used as a guide for later cases
vocabulary.definition: a earlier judicial decision that guides later cases

vocabulary.translation: to set aside an earlier decision
vocabulary.definition: to reject an earlier decision by a higher court

vocabulary.translation: to establish something firmly so it is hard to change
vocabulary.definition: to establish something so firmly that change is difficult
